author: Lucy Mangan
description:
The TikTok star describes them as a broke version of the Kardashians, but they are far too funny and charismatic for that. Channel 4 has hit the TV jackpot!

Channel 4 must have fallen on Trewley Precious and her family with sobbing gratitude. An articulate, charismatic gift to the camera who is also a member of the segment of the population with which the broadcaster has long been most pruriently fascinated. Jackpot!! I like to think of her standing there, in all her contoured, coiffed, lashed and fillered glory, patting the grovelling film-makers on the head with the satisfaction of knowing that her time has truly come.

Trewley Precious, if you have not had what I suspect is soon to be the inescapable pleasure, is an online influencer (nearly a million people follow her on TikTok) and member of the Traveller community who now stars – alongside her four siblings and their magisterial mother Tina – in the new reality series Secret Lives of Gypsy Wives. Trewley describes
title: Secret Lives of Gypsy Wives review – Trewley Precious and her glorious family are a gift to reality TV

description:
The new prime minister has promised a ‘circuit breaker’ moment for the country, as he becomes the UK’s seventh leader since 2016. But will he be able to make the changes that are desperately needed? Pippa Crerar and Kiran Stacey look at how he will try to do things differently and who will be helping him in the cabinet

Please keep sending your comments and questions to Pippa and Kiran at politicsweeklyuk@theguardian.com

author: Kiran Stacey Policy editor
description:
Choice of John Healey for chancellor shocks insiders after weeks of fierce lobbying on behalf of party big hitters

  • UK politics live – latest updates

For weeks, as ministers jostled, lobbied and positioned themselves for big jobs in an Andy Burnham government, the incoming prime minister remained sphinxlike. He told an interviewer on Monday that he had a black box containing his ministerial picks and major policy announcements, adding that even as he prepared to enter Downing Street: “The black box is still sealed.”

And so, when John Healey was appointed chancellor on Monday after intense briefing from allies of Ed Miliband, Shabana
title: Briefing wars: how Labour ministers tried, and failed, to get into Burnham’s cabinet

author: Editorial
description:
Outside Downing Street, Britain’s new prime minister struck the right notes. Now he and his cabinet need to be brave

A 1970s adage attributed to the former Tory chancellor Reginald Maudling maintained that Britain was essentially a Conservative country that sometimes voted Labour. That was always a questionable assertion, given the defining postwar role of Labour in shaping a fairer social settlement. But the trauma of successive election victories by Margaret Thatcher from 1979 onwards meant that senior figures on the centre left began to think along similar lines; a sometimes debilitating caution crept into the leadership of a party founded to ser
title: The Guardian view on Andy Burnham’s first day: the right vision, but time is of the essence | Editorial

author: Editorial
description:
Literature, the arts and social sciences must not be sacrificed as higher education funding is squeezed

“I ask nothing more from you than to do what you have been doing. Go out into the fray and keep reading,” was Percival Everett’s advice when he addressed graduating students at Wesleyan university in Connecticut last summer. Fitting words from a prize-winning novelist, at a time when gambling has become a more common leisure activity in the US than reading a book. In the UK, too, concerns are growing about the decline of reading, partly due to ubiquitous screen-based entertainment. Last week, parliament’s education committee called for the National Year o
title: The Guardian view on humanities cuts in universities: academic departments are more than cost centres | Editorial

author: Rowena Mason and Peter Walker
description:
From the Treasury to the Home Office, we look at who is heading up key departments in new PM’s government

  • UK politics live – latest updates

  • Burnham vows his arrival in power will be ‘circuit breaker’ moment for UK

  • Six highlights from Andy Burnham’s first Downing Street speech

Andy Burnham has appointed his first cabinet, with the new prime minister rewarding those who have been loyal to his takeover efforts. He had promised to pick his top team from all wings of the party in an effort to show he is trying
title: Andy Burnham’s first Labour cabinet: who’s in and who’s out?

author: Stephen Bates
description:
Presenter of BBC Radio 4’s Today programme whose sacking caused outrage among his loyal listeners

For many listeners to Radio 4, the broadcaster and journalist Edward Stourton, who has died aged 68 of prostate cancer, epitomised all that they valued most about the BBC. His voice was authoritative, unflappable and unmistakably posh, even stately; his questioning in interviews courteous but incisive; and his range of knowledge and insight unimpeachable.

These were all reasons why when Stourton – always known as Ed – was unexpectedly effectively sacked from presenting the Today programme in 2008 that there was such a backlash from newspapers, especially of the right, and the programme’s devoted followers. This was caused not least by the corporation’s brusque and clumsy handling of the ending of his contract, about which he was informed while away from the office by a Daily Mail journalist ringing up to
title: Edward Stourton obituary

title: Ben Jennings on Andy Burnham becoming prime minister – cartoon

author: Polly Toynbee
description:
He looks the part, with a rise as impressive as his speeches, but is that enough? You cannot know if someone is up to the job until they have to do it

Only vaulting ambition takes anyone to No 10, but Andy Burnham’s ambition reaches phenomenal heights. Can he really make the biggest changes in 40 years? Can he build a new economy? The new prime minister lashes himself to the mast of those mighty aspirations, but adds in something even riskier – an end to rough sleeping, ordered immediately. That’s so highly visible everywhere that it will be a test of the extent of his power – will it reach into each dank alley and shop doorway?

He understands the immensity of the tasks ahead. “I know what to do,” he said on taking u
title: With PM Burnham, we’ll get warmth, audacity and knowhow. For everything else, cling to hope | Polly Toynbee

Andy Burnham has become the sixth UK prime minister in a decade after a transfer of power from his predecessor Keir Starmer. In his first address outside Downing Street, he said his arrival in power would be a ‘circuit breaker’ moment for Britain and that his government will bring the ‘biggest changes in 40 years’. Lucy Hough speaks to political correspondent Alexandra Topping

title: Andy Burnham becomes Britain’s new prime minister - The Latest

description:
Tens of thousands of protesters have defied police orders and descended on Delhi to demand the resignation of India’s education minister in one of the largest anti-government demonstrations in years

title: India’s Cockroach party supporters march on parliament in New Delhi

author: Nicole Carpenter
description:
The developer of Duck Detective reveals details of her ‘sad grandma game’ follow-up: a whodunnit – or who-plans-to-do-it? – with a darker edge

Someone wants to kill grandma. In this Knives Out-inspired mystery game, each of your family members is suspicious in their own way: your stressed mum, your “midlife crisis uncle” and especially that stranger in your bedroom. Yikes!

While Apple Crumble is still a mystery, it is mechanically different from Happy Broccoli Games’ previous game, Duck Detective, in which the player solves crimes in a small office. Here you are largely snooping through your family home. “I love the idea of having a walking sim where you can really open up every drawer, every door, and see what’s behind there,” says founder and creative dire
title: Apple Crumble: a tasty Knives Out-inspired mystery that lets you snoop on your own family

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Readers on the pros and cons of the government’s plan to give cohabiting partners marriage-like rights

Ruth Deech’s article opposing cohabitation law reform overlooks the reality faced by 3.5 million cohabiting couples in the UK who are not married (David Lammy’s proposed cohabitation law would be bad for couples – and worse for some women, 14 July). While she argues that couples who choose not to marry should not acquire legal rights automatically, the current system of no rights leaves too many vulnerable people, particularly women and children, without meaningful protection when a relationship ends or a partner dies. Many still mistakenly believe in the myth of “common law marriage”. The proposals aim to strike a balance between respecting autonomy and protecting vulnerable people.

The law must reflect modern life. Many couples raise
title: Will a cohabitation law be bad for couples? | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Ruth Wilkinson on employers’ need to safeguard staff during heatwaves, and Christine Özden on keeping children safe in overheated schools

Hannah Spencer’s proposal for maximum workplace temperatures (Green MP Hannah Spencer to introduce bill on maximum workplace temperatures, 12 July) highlights an increasingly urgent issue for employers and policymakers alike. While legislation may help provide clarity in the future, businesses should not wait for a maximum legal limit before acting to protect workers.

Extreme temperatures can have a serious impact on worker health and safety as they can impair concentration and increase fatigue, both of which raise the likelihood of accidents.
title: British workplaces and schools have to adapt to keep employees and pupils safe | Letters

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Manchester’s integrated care board offers the health service a domestic alternative to the US firm, says Dr Devan Moodley

Regarding Peter Geoghegan’s article (I investigated Palantir’s foothold in the British state – and what I found should worry us all, 15 July), the nine years that Greater Manchester’s health system has spent without Palantir is a result not of caution but bold conviction.

Greater Manchester’s integrated care board remains the only one in England to decline the Palantir-built federated data platform, having concluded that its own homegrown data capability was stronger. It built that capability with British universities, NHS clinicians and domestic technology firms.

Continue reading...<
title: Palantir isn’t the only option for the NHS | Letter

author: Zoe Williams
description:
Young, old, midlife – whatever your age, gender or sector, the unemployment crisis is hitting us all. The only way through it is together

The personal experience of long-term unemployment is one people rarely share, for completely understandable reasons. There’s a bit of superstition that saying it out loud will bed it in, and there’s always one person in 100 who will choose to explain away the misfortune as your own personal failing.

Even if they’re clearly in the grip of superstitions of their own – trying to ward off your fate for themselves – it’s hard not to take criticism personally in such a personal situation. The conventions of human interaction are that you shouldn’t really mention a cloud unless you have a silver lining handy. For instance: after the financial crash in 2008, I remember hearing a couple interviewed on the radio who had both been made redundant when the private school they worked for closed down. After describing months of fruitless job applica
title: Welcome to the age of extreme job anxiety | Zoe Williams

author: Guardian Staff
description:
Urban transport policies and residential design need to respect outdoor play as a vital necessity for children, says Ellen Weaver

In the brilliant Swiss research cited by Lenore Skenazy (If you want your kids to thrive this summer, don’t just turn off their phones – open your front door, too, 15 July), young children playing unsupervised was culturally accepted and normal. The children in the Swiss study who did not play outside independently were prevented from doing so by traffic.

Yes, we need to relieve parents of the horrendous pressure of cultural expectati
title: Ensure children can play outside independently | Letter

author: Alex Bellos
description:
The answer to today’s puzzle

Earlier today I set you a puzzle about keeping homes cool in a heatwave. Here it is again with the solution.

Imagine a room with a set of curtains. When the Sun is shining, its energy comes through the windows where it is absorbed by the curtains. The curtains get hotter and hotter until they reach a temperature at which they are radiating as much heat as they absorb. The curtains radiate 50 per cent of this heat back towards the window, and 50 per cent of the heat into the room.

Continue reading...
title: Did you solve it? Do you think like a physicist?

author: Eddy Frankel
description:
Trent Park, London
A new museum in this redeveloped country house relives its fascinating period as a palatial prison of war camp – with Jewish refugees listening in from the basement

History happened here. I mean, history happens everywhere. But serious, important, world-shaping history happened at Trent Park.

Built on the grounds of Enfield Chase, an expanse of Hertfordshire countryside used as hunting grounds by royalty, this country house has lived many lives. It was a Georgian retreat, a Victorian mansion, a post-Edwardian sanctuary, and then, during the second world war, it became a place of secrets. Afterwards, it became a university campus, before falling into dereliction. Now, it has been revived, and its hidden stories brought into the light.

Continue reading...
title: Trent Park House of Secrets review – the bugged stately home where German prisoners blabbed their secrets

author: John Crace
description:
Rapid turnover of prime ministers continues as UK gets another promise that, this time, things will be different

  • UK politics live – latest updates

Not another one. It would be no surprise to find out that overseas tour companies now include package holiday visits to watch the UK’s rapid turnover of prime ministers. “Come to London to watch the motorcade nearly run over a group of fancy dress soldiers playing a Bon Jovi medley just outside Buckingham Palace.” Two years is a long time in the lifetime of a UK leader. Liz Truss was in and out in seconds. Our buy one, get one free prime minister. In Britain, we sure know how to Dance Me to the End of Love.

Still, practice makes perfect and we now have the handover of power nailed to a T. Everyone knows exactly wha
title: No tears from Keir as Burnham strolls into No 10 with the clock already ticking | John Crace

author: Michael Savage Media editor
description:
Media regulator to take no action despite receiving 446 complaints about comments by Bev Turner

GB News will not be investigated by the media regulator after a presenter insisted there was no riot in Belfast last month, despite cars and houses being set alight, attacks on police and families fleeing their homes.

Ofcom received more than 400 complaints following the comments by Bev Turner, presenter of the broadcaster’s Late Show Live, who said there “weren’t riots” and that no houses had been burnt in the violent disorder.

Continue reading...
title: GB News will not be investigated over ‘no riot in Belfast’ claim

author: Rob Draper
description:
The former England manager may be remembered by many for his ‘I’d love it’ rant in 1996, but that should not obscure the remarkable nature of his football career

Kevin Keegan, who has died aged 75, is the only British player to win the Ballon d’Or twice, was the star of Liverpool’s first European Cup-winning team, a messianic figure at Newcastle United as a player and coach, forging a team so memorable that Fifas president wrote to commend him, and the only Englishman to both captain and manage the men’s national team. And yet, as Keegan would ruefully reflect, he will principally be remembered by many for an emotional outburst that precipitated Newcastle’s historic failure in a Premier League title race, a TV interview which presaged the coming era of the modern game.
title: A pioneer and a superstar, Kevin Keegan’s achievements were extraordinary

author: Guardian Staff
description:
The UK is a nation of animal lovers. But the rise of ‘barkitecture’ has taken it too far, with people investing in outdoor showers, whirlpool baths and ergonomic feeding stations for their faithful friends

Name: Barkitecture.

Age: 27 years old.

Appearance: Plush provisions for posh pooches.

It’s 27 years old? That’s hardly newsworthy. Well, there was Fred Albert’s 1999 book Barkitecture, about upmarket kennels. And then there was the 2020 Quibi platform show Barkitecture, where a Bachelorette runner-up made kennels for celebrities. Also, the Guardian has covered the term before.

Continue reading...
title: Barking mad: why would someone spend £28,000 on a home spa for their dog?

author: Erica Jeal
description:
Glyndebourne, East Sussex
The director hits perfectly all the comic marks of Strauss’s opera about an opera, but there’s few insights in a work that should be moving as well as frothy and fun.

Glyndebourne’s new productions this summer have followed a theme: first Tosca, about a fictional opera singer; then L’Orfeo, about the mythical musician. Now comes Richard Strauss’s Ariadne auf Naxos – an opera about an opera. It starts with the shenanigans backstage as two troupes – one high art, one low – prepare after-dinner entertainment for their rich patron, then the performance that ensues when they are forced to combine their acts. The real subject is, of course, love – and that comes across only pa
title: Ariadne auf Naxos review – Laurent Pelly’s staging has plenty of wit but lacks weight

description:
You told us your tried-and-tested tricks for keeping children entertained. Plus, the best eye masks and natural deodorants, tested

• Don’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up here

If there’s one thing worse than a long journey, it’s a long journey with bored, fractious children. So what helps smooth things along? We asked for your best, tried-and-tested hacks for travelling with kids, from “fidget bags” to lollipops.

On a long car trip from the UK to France with his kids, reader Tim Leadbeater attached small plastic baskets with string around the pillars of the front headrest: “They held everything from felt tips to half-eaten food, not only preventing stains on covers but also keeping everything rea

World premieres of films led by Helen Mirren, Seth Rogen and Chris Rock lead the lineup for this year’s Toronto film festival.

• United get club-record fee of about £850,000 for forward

Chelsea have announced the signing of the France forward Melvine Malard from Manchester United on a four-year contract. The Guardian revealed last week that a deal was close for the 26-year-old, who has left United after three seasons for about £850,000.

Malard had one year on her contract and United were keen to keep the forward. However, once it became clear Malard wanted a move United decided to sell rather than lose a high-value player on a free next summer.

author: Neha Gohil Midlands correspondent
description:
Drivers in West Midlands say buses ‘unbearable’ during heatwaves, raising employee and passenger safety fears

Bus drivers in the West Midlands have spoken out about the “horrendous” working conditions they have experienced during heatwaves, which led to 40C temperatures in their cabs.

The UK was hit by high temperatures and dry weather in three successive heatwaves, with temperatures topping 37C last month when the country recorded its hottest ever June day. Last week, the Met Office warned climate extremes were becoming the “new ‘normal’ for the UK”.

title: ‘My shirt was wringing’: National Express bus drivers speak out on 40C conditions

author: Ashifa Kassam
description:
Judit Polgár to discuss role with prime minister, who says Hungary needs someone the whole nation is proud of

Hungary’s prime minister, Péter Magyar, has announced plans to ask Judit Polgár, widely considered the greatest female chess player of all time, to take on the largely ceremonial role of president.

Magyar said he would meet Polgár on Monday to discuss the matter. “Our country needs unity, peace and a president that all Hungarians can be proud of,” he wrote on social media. “Judit Polgár’s name has been synonymous with talent and perseverance for decades.”

Continue reading...
title: Strategic move by Magyar as he picks chess prodigy for president

author: Sam Jones in Madrid
description:
• El Mundo marks country’s ‘unique collective experience’

  • El Pais highlights the side’s ‘conviction of hard work’

Sometimes football is about more than just football. As Spain’s still-breathless media pointed out on Monday, the national side’s victory against Argentina the previous night was an epochal event that had transcended talk of tactics, grumbles over hydration breaks and displays of distinctly ungentlemanly conduct.

“It is the triumph of Luis de la Fuente and of an extraordinary group of footballers who – in a sport of stars and social media divas – have prioritised team values, joint intelligence, and the conviction of hard work,” said an editorial in El País.

title: ‘A unique collective experience’: Spain media hail team’s World Cup triumph

author: Alexandra Coghlan
description:
Royal Albert Hall, London
Outgoing chief conductor David Afkham brought Spanish repertoire, castanets and a certain team’s football scarf in a programme heavy with national treasures

What a night for Spain. No, not because of sporting happenings in New Jersey, but because – nearly 90 years since their founding – their National Orchestra finally made their Proms debut under chief conductor David Afkham to a packed Royal Albert Hall. It was a beginning, but also a celebratory end: Afkham hands over the baton to Kent Nagano next season. They came prepared, suitcases stuffed with Spanish repertoire and castanets – oh, and a certain team’s football scarf, as modelled by Afkham during the encore.

Afkham’s more than a decade with the orchestra hit its heights with Spanish repertoire, building on a legacy that earned the ensemble a Latin Grammy for best f
title: Spanish National Orchestra/Afkham review – Proms debut sees orchestra’s celebrations kick off early

author: Lydia Spencer-Elliott
description:
The latest in our series of writers picking their most meaningful comfort watches is a tribute to the inspiring power of the 1996 Roald Dahl adaptation

When I think about what makes me feel good, it isn’t fantasy or escapism; it’s justice, morality and triumph – sizing up to a bully bigger than you and prevailing against the odds. I never fail to be charmed by the story of an underdog, someone who shouldn’t win but finds a way through resilience, determination or sometimes a genius loophole and a little bit of magic, and no film hits those attributes harder for me than Danny DeVito’s Matilda.

The zany adaptation of Roald Dahl’s 1988 children’s novel came out in cinemas in December 1996, four months after I came into the world. The film, set (unlike the supremely British source text) in a leopard-print-clad edition of suburban California, focuses on the titular character (played by Mara Wilson), who grows up unseen and unheard by her grifter, TV-obsessed parents, Harry a
title: ‘Justice, morality and triumph’: why Matilda is my feelgood movie

author: Amy Fleming
description:
For those who are burned out, perimenopausal, or both, dancing all night can be a panacea. It’s great exercise, lowers stress, boosts energy and provides connection. No wonder so many are doing it

It’s 4am and I’m in a club – the first time I’ve done this in years. I’m 51 and in my sandwich era, meaning I’ve got teenage and elderly loved ones on my mind – a situation that generally calls for early nights. But when you’re responsibilities-maxxing, sometimes you need the opposite. A blowout. A huge, transcendent, resetting release. A rave.

I don’t know what took me so long to get around to it. Misplaced parental guilt? Internalised ageism? Exhaustion? It’s not as though I didn’t know other gen-Xers who have been regularly getting blissfully – ceremonially, even – lost in house, techno or drum’n’bass, and they’re not alone. A 2025 study by the University of Leeds went viral: “
title: The rave secret: why middle-aged women are larging it – and seeing big health benefits

author: Anna Tims
description:
I bought a wheelchair for my daughter, but she later died in hospital and the company refuses a refund

I bought a £435 wheelchair for my disabled daughter from my local Lifestyle & Mobility store.

She had been admitted to hospital for tests and I planned to use the chair to take her on outings when she was discharged.

Continue reading...
title: Why can’t Lifestyle & Mobility store show compassion after my loss?

description:
Laura Donnelly’s DI Kennedy thinks she has guessed the next victim but can she save him? Plus, sex, chicks and ostriches in Chris Packham’s Evolution

9pm, ITV1
With the serial killer taking their third victim in the last cliffhanger, it’s been a rough week at work for DI Kennedy (Laura Donnelly) in this sinister detective drama. Local men in their teens and 20s are the targets, and Kennedy thinks she knows who the next one will be – but will she save him? Or is she just playing into the killer’s sick, twisted game? And what about her own worrying home dilemma with her daughter? Hollie Richardson

author: Jo Khan
description:
⚽ Latest World Cup news as tournament comes to close
⚽ Player guide | Golden Boot | Follow on TikTok | Mail us

It was the triumph of an idea, an identity. Of an unshakable and patient faith. And when it was over, Spain’s new generation having emulated the one from the 2010 World Cup, all of those legendary names, there was simply delirium for them.

It’s over. 104 matches later and Spain have been crowned world champions after defeating Argentina 1-0 in extra time. In contrast to the goal-fest that was England’s third-place wi
title: World Cup 2026: latest news and reaction after Spain beat Argentina to win trophy

author: Stuart Clark
description:
The full constellation can be frustrating to track down in the UK owing to its low presence in the southern sky

This week we will take the opportunity to identify Scorpius, the Scorpion, one of the famous zodiacal constellations.

In mythology, Scorpius is the creature sent to kill Orion, the hunter. The two constellations are therefore on opposite sides of the sky from one another, so that when Scorpius rises, Orion has already departed.

Continue reading...
title: Starwatch: Identifying the Scorpion, mythical adversary of Orion

author: Kate Blincoe
description:
Caistor St Edmund, Norfolk: Underfoot the ground is as hard as metal, while the council’s ‘leaky dams’ are set for the next deluge

Catkins fall from the sweet chestnut trees like long yellow streamers from a party. More than 20 wasps fret over the bonnet of my car, feeding off something – maybe sticky tree sap or dead insects.

The hay crop is in. No high yields, but better than last year. Two red kites hunt over the coumarin-sweet cut meadows and the swallows glide low. The empty fields usually beckon a gallop, but the ground rings out under hoof like a metalled road. If there is no rain, a second crop seems unlikely.

Continue reading...
title: Country diary: Beaver-style flood defences take root amid a hosepipe ban | Kate Blincoe

author: Michael O'Flaherty
description:
Without iron-clad legal safeguards, offshore migration centres can only repeat the worst mistakes of the recent past

Europe has entered a new era of outsourced migration management. After a vote by the European parliament, the EU’s return regulation is nearing adoption – promising “more efficient” returns and “swifter” procedures to deport unwanted migrants. This will give countries the legal runway to set up return hubs – that is, offshore facilities to process people deemed to have no right to stay in the EU.

Despite opposition from countries such as Spain and France – and an outcry from rights groups – many other governments appear anxious to join in. An
title: Europe is at risk of creating a human rights black hole with its ‘return hubs’ for migrants | Michael O'Flaherty

author: Michael Hogan
description:
A pranked England manager, a bored Beckham, a Viking takeover and an unwise Wayne Rooney wager: here are the TV treasures of the beautiful game’s biggest ever tournament

A stodgy final saw silky Spain deservedly beat cynical Argentina. Football wasn’t coming home after all as England suffered semi-final heartbreak again, before salvaging some pride to finish third – their best World Cup finish since 1966. The Tartan Army drank America’s bars dry as their team went out with a whimper. Cape Verde lasted longer than Germany. It was the end of the road for Ronaldo and Modric, while the phrase “hydration break” entered everyday parlance. But beyond the pitch, it has been an eventful five weeks, too.

Here are 26 viral World Cup moments you might have missed …

Continue reading...
title: From Gary Lineker’s revenge to the bizarre tale of a missing cat: the best viral TV moments of the World Cup

author: Steve Rose
description:
At 78, the king of horror and sci-fi movies is as much of a rebel as ever. He talks about creativity, compromise (he’s not a fan) and how he became addicted to moviemaking

In 2024, John Carpenter had a dream that sounds like one of his movies: it involved a portal to the underworld beneath a disused church, monstrous demons and people being turned inside out. “I woke up and thought: wow! What an elaborate story,” he says. “I rarely have cinematic dreams, but this was one of them.” He liked it so much that he has turned it into a graphic novel, Cathedral, with an accompanying soundtrack. “It seemed to fit this heavy metal groove that we were starting on, and it worked out pretty well.”

Most people would consider this a nightmare rather than a dream, I suggest. “No. Nightmares, for me, are personal – something that happened to me,” he replies. “Usually my nightmares are, I’m directing a movie and no one will listen to me. No one will follow my directions. Seriously, that’
title: ‘Everything I know about evil I learned in that small town’: John Carpenter on terrifying the world with Halloween, The Thing and The Fog

author: Owen Hatherley
description:
The Manifesta biennale is taking over a dozen tiny churches in German towns ravaged by division and decline – and filling them with ball games, bouncy castles and a radical community spirit

After Germany’s Ruhr conurbation – the third-largest urban area in western Europe – was pummelled during the second world war, planners came up with an ingenious idea. About 80% of the sprawl – which incorporates big cities such as Essen and Duisburg, and dozens of smaller towns like Bochum and Gelsenkirchen – had been destroyed. And so, for the reconstruction, a newly formed Diocese of the Ruhr built literally hundreds of closely packed Pantoffelkirchen or “slipper churches”, so named because they were close enough to housing developments for churchgoers to walk to mass in their slippers.

Today, Pantoffelkirchen are declining sharply. Estimates of the amount of disused or derelict churches are as high as 300, and 100 have been sold off in the last year alone. Unti
title: A Ruhr treat: can a giant pigeon and a pink basketball revive Germany’s depressed industrial heartland?

author: Patrick Greenfield
description:
Experts warn increase in enhanced photos on birding platforms creating fake sightings, threatening credibility of tool used by scientists

For many birdwatchers, recording a species outside its normal range is the holy grail. In the UK, the discoveries often make national headlinesThe western reef heron, for example, usually found in Africa and southern Europe, spotted in a seaside town in north Wales in June, which was widely celebrated on birding forums.

But a new scourge is threatening to disrupt the fun: AI slop.

title: Al-altered images on birdwatching forums putting research at risk
